newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition draws big crowd, police relent.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition draws big crowd, police relent.

text.p: Serbian opposition supporters flooded the capital Belgrade on Tuesday evening as police apparently gave up trying to keep protesters off city streets.

Beating drums and blowing whistles, tens of thousands of demonstrators from outlying districts converged on the city centre for a daily protest demanding ruling Socialists recognise results of local elections.

Riot police over the past week had formed cordons on city streets to force protesters onto pavements. But the police relented on Tuesday evening, allowing marchers to block traffic and cross a main bridge spanning the Sava river.

Leaders of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition were buoyed at the turnout and said it showed that 10 straight weeks of protests were gaining momentum and wearing out the police -- not the demonstrators.
"There is no police cordon which can hold back a Serbia which knows what it wants -- our future, democracy, a renaissance of Serbia," said Vuk Draskovic, one of the Zajedno leaders.
Protests have swept Belgrade and other major towns since President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists refused to concede defeat in November local polls and annulled results.
The opposition, raising the stakes in its political confrontation with Milosevic, earlier formed a rival government in the provincial town of Smederevska Palanka, 80 km (50 miles) south of Belgrade.
Zajedno swore in a town council in a street ceremony in the town after police prevented them from entering the municipal building along with 230 supporters.
Inside, Milosevic's Socialist party convened its version of the new town council with a leftist majority which Zajedno says was obtained by fraud.
Zajedno said it might use the same tactic in Belgrade and other towns where its victories were overturned by authorities.
Later, police beat opposition supporters holding their daily rally in Smederevska Palanka, a Zajedno official alleged.
The local head of Zajedno, Ljubisa Brkic, required medical treatment after he was hit on the chin and stomach, the official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters by telephone.
Smederevska Palanka was among 14 Serbian towns where opposition victories in local elections were voided by the Socialists on grounds of unspecified "irregularities".
The United States has led Western condemnation of Milosevic's handling of the crisis, protesting against police beatings and demanding his party accept election results.
Russian First Deputy Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov, whose government enjoys friendly relations with Serbia, met Milosevic and Zajedno representatives this week to promote a compromise.
After Milosevic met Ivanov on Tuesday, the state Tanjug news agency said the two agreed that a state's internal problems should not be resolved by "external interference".
State television has accused opposition leaders of plotting with foreign powers and ethnic Albanians in the southern province of Kosovo to "destabilise" Serbia.
The protests have exposed divisions within Milosevic's ranks and criticism from the republic of Montenegro, Serbia's junior partner in the Yugoslav federation.

Socialist officials, trying to defuse the political crisis, have promised a "reshuffle" of government posts. They announced on Tuesday the sacking of the directors of the state power and telephone companies.
Milosevic's delaying tactics, media attacks and police cordons have so far failed to stifle the protests and Zajedno leaders said the former communist party chief was irreparably damaged.
"This regime is already dead, and Serbia will never be the same again -- we don't know the exact date it will fall, but it will be soon," Vesna Pesic, another Zajedno co-leader, told the crowd.
